name: Hana Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Northfield Farm for the Visser brothers, Pieter and Johan. It's about 150 beef cattle and a lot of potatoes. I'm in by half seven, I feed the cattle with Johan, bed them up with straw, and from October to March I'm on the potato grading line, picking out the rotten ones and the stones.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up at Northfield?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I worked thirty years at Dahl's Hardware on the high street, keys and paint and screws. Old Mr Dahl retired in 2022 and nobody wanted the shop. My son knew Pieter, and Pieter needed someone for the grading line, so at 54 I started over. I'm still slow with the cattle; Johan does the tricky ones.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's simple: the cattle are fed or they're not. The grading line wears me out, standing in the cold shed for eight hours staring at potatoes. My husband Lars drives a lorry hauling grain and livestock, and his back isn't great, so I worry about that more than my own feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but quietly. People get excited about every new thing. At work I'd say right, back to the potatoes, and I'm not online much except to look at the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, and nothing changing isn't nothing. We've four years left on the mortgage, Lars's back is going, and Pieter keeps talking about buying an optical sorter for the potatoes. That kind of machine already exists, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Northfield as long as they'll have me. We'd cut back a bit, fewer meals out, and put the difference towards the mortgage. And I'd tell Lars to see the doctor about his back before it decides for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it's always there in the background, like a dripping tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the optical sorter Pieter mentions.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pieter showed me a video of one at a farm show. A camera looks at every potato and a little puff of air knocks the bad ones off. If Pieter (her boss) buys an optical sorter, my whole winter job goes, and I'd be back to just feeding cattle. That's half the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would half the hours mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd manage the mortgage but nothing else. No new boiler, no trip to see our eldest son. I'd rather not think about it, honestly, until Pieter actually signs for it.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, quietly, because people get excited about every new thing.
At work I'd say **back to the potatoes**; I'm hardly online except for the grandchildren.
think: Nothing changing isn't nothing: **four years** of mortgage and Lars's bad back remain.
Pieter's talk of an **optical sorter** threatens my winter job whether AI arrives or not.
do: Keep working at **Northfield** as long as the Vissers will have me.
Cut **meals out** and put the savings towards the mortgage.
Push Lars to see the **doctor** about his back before it decides for him.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a **dripping tap** in the background, though not scared.
S0.quote: If Pieter (her boss) buys an optical sorter, my whole winter job goes, and I'd be back to just feeding cattle.
fieldNote: Her real threat is an **existing machine**, the optical sorter, not AI.
Household pressures are **Lars's back** and the last four years of the mortgage.
She prefers **not to think** about bad news until it is certain.

steps.text: Keep working the grading line and cattle at Northfield
Cut meals out and put the money on the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use it for paperwork but leave the real jobs alone. At work I'd say to Johan it's the office girls in town who should worry, not us. Online, nothing; I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the Vissers would use it to plan the cheapest way to run the place. The AI would tell Pieter the sorter pays for itself in two years, and he'd buy it. And Lars's haulage firm would have AI booking the loads and squeezing the drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what Pieter decides before I do anything drastic. Meanwhile I'd put an extra hundred a month into savings, so if the winter job goes we have a cushion. I'd keep turning up and working hard, so I'm the one they keep for the cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see it coming in my own shed. I don't like change and I'm too old to learn computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're too old to learn computers. Is that true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not too old, but too tired. I spent thirty years learning screws and paint at the hardware shop, and I'm still learning cattle, so my head's full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lars if his firm started using AI for the bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband Lars to keep his head down and not argue with the computer. He's 60 and he'll want to argue. He'd say a machine can't know which farmer's yard has a tight gate.

say: AI is fine for **paperwork**, but it should leave the real jobs alone.
The **office workers** in town should worry, not farm hands like us.
think: AI would tell Pieter the **sorter pays** for itself in two years, and he'd buy it.
Lars's **haulage firm** would use AI to book loads and squeeze the drivers.
do: Wait to see what **Pieter decides** before doing anything drastic.
Put an extra **hundred a month** into savings in case the winter job goes.
Work hard at Northfield so I'm the one they **keep for cattle**.
feel: **Anxious**, because I can see the change coming in my own **shed**.
**Tired**, with no room left in my head for computers.
S1.quote: I spent thirty years learning screws and paint at the hardware shop, and I'm still learning cattle, so my head's full.
fieldNote: She expects AI planning to **speed up** Pieter's decision on the sorter.
Two household incomes face pressure: her **grading hours** and Lars's driving.
She avoids technology from **fatigue** more than principle.

steps.text: Wait for Pieter's decision on the optical sorter
Keep working hard on the cattle so the Vissers keep me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let it happen that fast, and somebody in government should slow it down. At work I'd say to Johan we're done for. Online I still wouldn't say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? By 2031 a robot feeds the cattle and drives Lars's lorry. I'm 63 and he's 65, and the mortgage only finishes in 2030. We'd both be out of work before the pension, and I don't know how we'd pay for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything now: the second car, the satellite TV, the trip to see our eldest son. Every spare penny goes into savings until the mortgage is gone. And I'd sit the boys down and ask if they could help us out if it comes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It would keep me up at night. I already lie awake about Lars's back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In those three years before the robots come, what's different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are when we'd scrape. The AI would already be doing Pieter's planning, and he'd probably buy the sorter by 2029. So I'd lose the winter grading first and then the cattle feeding in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it feel asking your sons for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Horrible. You raise your sons so they don't have to worry about you, and now I'd be asking them for help. But Mikkel, our youngest, earns well as a plumber, and he'd want us to ask.

say: It's **madness** to let it happen that fast; government should slow it down.
To Johan on the yard I'd say **we're done for**.
think: By **2031** a robot feeds the cattle and drives Lars's lorry, before either of us reaches pension.
The **mortgage** only ends in 2030, so we'd be stretched to pay anything.
do: Cut the **second car**, the satellite TV and the trip to our eldest son now.
Put every **spare penny** into savings until the mortgage is gone.
Ask our sons, especially **Mikkel**, whether they could help us if needed.
feel: **Alarmed** and awake at night, on top of the worry about Lars's back.
S2.quote: You raise your sons so they don't have to worry about you, and now I'd be asking them for help.
fieldNote: Both incomes go within the **three-year window**: her grading first, then cattle and Lars's lorry.
She expects the **sorter** to arrive by 2029 once AI is doing Pieter's planning.
Asking family is **painful** but realistic, as Mikkel earns well as a plumber.

steps.text: Sell the second car and cancel the satellite TV
Put every spare penny into savings until the mortgage ends
Ask our son Mikkel whether he could help if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. At work I'd tell Johan we'll see how it goes. I still wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots in 2034 I'm 66 and Lars is 68, so we'd both have reached the pension. The mortgage is gone by 2030. The AGI in 2031 might still bring the sorter in earlier, but it's not the same cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what Pieter does, like I always do. I'd keep saving the extra hundred a month, so if the winter job goes in 2031 we can cover the gap. Nothing more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Better than the fast one. I could sleep, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait and see. Is there a point where you'd act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Pieter signs for the sorter, then I'd act, but only then. I'd ask him for more cattle hours or look at the potato packers in town. I won't jump before I'm pushed, because leaving the hardware shop was never my choice anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lars think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lars says he'll be retired before any robot can reverse a lorry into the Vissers' yard. He's probably right. That yard gate is very tight.

say: I'd tell Johan **we'll see** how it goes, and still not post a thing.
think: With robots in **2034** Lars and I both reach the pension first.
AGI in 2031 might bring the **sorter** earlier, but it's not the same cliff.
do: Wait to see what **Pieter does** about the sorter before changing anything.
Keep saving the **extra hundred** a month to cover a gap from 2031.
S3.quote: I won't jump before I'm pushed, because leaving the hardware shop was never my choice anyway.
fieldNote: Five years of warning puts both their **pension ages** before the robots.
She keeps her **wait-and-see** stance and names one clear trigger: the sorter.
Humour about the **tight yard gate** shows her mood lifting.

steps.text: Wait for Pieter's decision on the sorter before acting
Keep saving an extra 100 a month for a gap from 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change. At work I'd say it's not our problem. I'd stay off the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It won't touch my job; I'll be retired long before 2039. But the everyday worries stay: Lars's back, the mortgage until 2030, the sorter Pieter keeps talking about. AI isn't the only thing that can take a job; a potato sorter can do that today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Northfield till 66, same as now. I'd wait and see on the sorter. That's all; I'm not one for big plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the same as today. Not about AI, about ordinary things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your grandchildren anything about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandchildren to learn a trade like their uncle Mikkel. Plumbers, electricians, people who come to your house. I'd say that whether there were robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good in this one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Lars's back gets a rest if robots load the lorries. If his back could get a rest, I'd be pleased, but it'll be too late for him by then.

say: **Ten years** is a long time, and lots can change.
At work I'd say it's **not our problem**.
think: My job is safe because I'll be **retired** long before 2039.
The **everyday worries** stay: Lars's back, the mortgage and Pieter's sorter.
do: Carry on at **Northfield** until 66, the same as now.
Wait and see whether Pieter buys the **sorter** before making plans.
feel: **Uneasy** as today, about ordinary things rather than AI.
S4.quote: AI isn't the only thing that can take a job; a potato sorter can do that today.
fieldNote: With a decade's warning, AI drops out, but the **existing pressures** keep her uneasy.
Her advice to grandchildren is **trades** that come to your house.
She sees little **upside** for herself, only a possible rest for Lars too late.

steps.text: Wait to see whether Pieter buys the sorter

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lars and I would both be out before the pension and before the mortgage is paid. What would help is letting older people take their pension early without losing half of it. And some warning from Pieter, honestly, a year's notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we already lost. The hardware shop is a phone shop now. People talk like AI is the first thing that ever took a job from a town, and it isn't.

headlineQuote: People talk like AI is the first thing that ever took a job from a town, and it isn't.
portrait: Hana is a **58-year-old** farmhand at Northfield who grades potatoes and feeds cattle after thirty years in a hardware shop.
She never uses AI and **waits and sees**, acting only when a decision like Pieter's sorter is made.
Her household carries **Lars's bad back** and a mortgage that runs to 2030, which keep her uneasy even without AI.
She turns **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, when both her and Lars's work would go before their pensions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as she and Lars would both lose work before the **pension** and mortgage end.
whatWouldHelp: Taking the **pension early** without losing half, and a year's **notice** from Pieter.
